books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, A. Slave Rebellions
Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, 1829

stimulus.text: "Let no man of us budge one step, and let slave-holders come to beat us from our country. America is more our country, than it is the whites—we have enriched it with our blood and tears." — David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, September 28, 1829
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, September 28, 1829). Wording checked against the Documenting the American South electronic edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker (1829)
stem: Walker addresses his Appeal to “my brethren,” his fellow Black Americans, rather than to white slaveholders. That choice of audience best shows that Walker

options.text: wanted Black readers to wake up and act for themselves
believed white slaveholders would free their slaves if asked politely
options.misconception: Walker speaks of slaveholders beating Black people from their country, not of polite requests.

options.text: wrote only for readers who already agreed with him
options.misconception: Walker says he wants to awaken slumbering brethren, people not yet acting.

options.text: thought the Declaration of Independence applied only to Black Americans
options.misconception: Walker quotes the Declaration to hold white Americans to their own words.

rationales.A: Walker calls his readers brethren and fellow citizens, and he wants to wake them to inquiry and action. Change starts with them.
rationales.B: Nothing in the passage asks slaveholders politely for anything. Walker warns them and calls on Black readers to stand firm.
rationales.C: Walker calls his brethren slumbering. He writes to wake people up, not only to cheer those already awake.
rationales.D: Walker quotes “all men are created equal” against white Americans. He claims the Declaration’s promise, he does not limit it.
rationales.general:
1. Note who Walker speaks to. He calls his readers brethren and fellow citizens.
2. Note what he asks of them. He wants to awaken a spirit of inquiry in them, not to persuade slaveholders.
3. Name the strategy. Change starts with Black readers acting for themselves.
Background: Walker was a free Black man in Boston who sold clothing and worked in reform causes.
Remember: always ask who a writer is talking to before asking what the writer wants.
